activities.anchor: Its logic is arbitrage, not opinion
activities.caption: call the carry — price the forward
activities.name: odForwardEstimate

config.prompt: Cash-and-carry: a stock trades at £100 and interest rates are 5% for one year. What is the fair one-year forward price, F = S·e^rT?
config.why: F = 100·e^0.05 ≈ 105.13 — exactly the cost of buying the stock now and carrying it, financed at 5%, to delivery. Any deviation is free money, which is why forward prices are arithmetic rather than forecasts.
config.context: If F is higher: sell the forward, buy the stock with borrowed funds. If lower, do the reverse.

activities.caption: pair each position with its view
activities.name: odStrategyMatch

config.prompt: Lego for payoff shapes — pair each position with the view it expresses:

pairs.right: a leveraged bull position with capped downside
portfolio insurance — a floor under held shares
a bet on volatility, not direction
insurance paid for by selling upside
limits both sides of the payoff

config.why: "What is your payoff diagram?" is the first professional question in any options conversation — and portfolio insurance's own 1987 crash story is the cautionary footnote.

activities.anchor: A cheap premium is not a bargain either
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the breakeven brief
activities.name: odBreakevenSpot

config.prompt: One line of this options-desk note is wrong — click it:
lines: Exercising a call above the strike is rational.
The premium was paid up front, before expiry.
Breakeven sits exactly at the strike.
A fund holding shares plus index puts has bought a floor.
Straddles bet on volatility rather than direction.
config.correction: Breakeven is strike plus premium — with the stock at 102, a call struck at 100 is exercised anyway and still nets a loss of 3.
config.why: In-the-money and profitable are different claims: the premium must be earned back first, and it is the market's no-arbitrage price of the payoff's time value.

config.text: Put-call parity: C − P = S − K·e^(−rT) — a long call plus a short %%0%% replicates a forward. With S = 100, K = 100 and r = 5% over one year, the right side is 100 − 95.12 = %%1%%.
config.hint: Long call + short put = long forward; 100·e^−0.05 ≈ 95.12.

activities.caption: pin the smile — where crash insurance sits
activities.name: odSmilePlace

config.prompt: The volatility smile: where is deep out-of-the-money crash insurance priced, relative to the lognormal model's prediction?
config.why: Systematically above — the smile/skew, a permanent scar from 1987 — so traders price volatility surfaces, not scalars, and implied volatility becomes a market of its own (the VIX, computed from index-option prices).

activities.anchor: The swap converts uncertainty into a chosen price of certainty
activities.caption: run the swap through both rate worlds
activities.name: odSwapBranch

config.root: You are treasurer. The company pays floating rates on £100m of debt and fears rises.

start.text: The bank quotes an interest-rate swap. Which leg do you pay?

choices.label: Pay 3.5% fixed, receive the floating index
choices.feedback: Fixed-for-floating: the classic hedge for a floating-rate borrower.

choices.label: Receive 3.5% fixed, pay floating
choices.feedback: That is the other side's trade — it would double your exposure to rising rates.

choices.label: No swap — keep the floating exposure
choices.feedback: A choice, but not a hedge: every rise in rates lands directly on the interest bill.

test.text: Over the swap's life, floating averages 4.5%. What is your effective borrowing cost?

choices.label: 3.5% — the floating leg pays you 1% back
choices.feedback: Exactly: receiving 4.5% while paying 3.5% fixed nets +1%, offsetting the rise.

choices.label: 4.5% — the swap cannot help
choices.feedback: It can: the swap nets +1% against the 3.5% fixed leg.

choices.label: Still 3.5% — you pay the 1% difference away
choices.feedback: The hedge holds in both directions: rates fell, the swap cost you 1%, the budget never moved.

choices.label: 2.5% — you pocket the cheap rates
choices.feedback: No — paying 3.5% fixed against 2.5% floating nets −1% this time. Effective cost unchanged.

end.text: Either way the cost is 3.5%: banks intermediate by quoting the fixed leg, and this swap market is the largest in the world by notional.

config.why: A swap exchanges payment streams — fixed-for-floating on a notional principal — turning uncertain financing costs into a budgeted one.

activities.caption: pair each Greek with its dial
activities.name: odGreekMatch

config.prompt: The risk dashboard has five dials — pair each Greek with what it measures:

pairs.right: price change per unit of underlying — runs 0 to 1, about 0.5 at-the-money
how fast delta itself changes — a short-gamma hedger buys high and sells low
time decay — accelerating in the final weeks for near-the-money strikes
sensitivity to implied volatility — a spike pays the holder regardless of direction
interest-rate sensitivity — minor for equity options, central for long-dated rates products

config.why: Risk limits are set per Greek because each dimension kills differently — direction, acceleration, decay, volatility — and desks keep smile-adjusted Greeks, stress-testing beyond the model.

activities.caption: bet before the reveal — in the money ≠ profitable
activities.name: odRetailPredict

config.q: You buy one call, strike £100, premium £5. At expiry the stock is £102 and you exercise. Your net result?
choices: +£2 — the option finished in the money
config.why: Exercising is rational above the strike, but the £5 premium was paid up front: breakeven is strike plus premium, so £102 nets −£3. In-the-money is not the same as profitable — and most retail options expire worthless besides.
